newsitem.title: USA: Bacteria in juice matched to western U.S. outbreak.
newsitem.headline: Bacteria in juice matched to western U.S. outbreak.

text.p: Researchers on Tuesday confirmed that dangerous bacteria found in Odwalla apple juice was genetically identical to microbes identified in an outbreak of food poisoning that has sickened 40 people.

The conclusion by scientists at the University of Washington provides the strongest evidence to date that tainted Odwalla juice was the source of an outbreak of the potentially fatal E.coli bacteria in Colorado, California, Washington and British Columbia.
"The evidence just keeps getting stronger and stronger," said Dr. John Kobayashi, senior epidemiologist with the Washington state Department of Health.

He said DNA "fingerprinting" by researchers showed that the virulent strain of E. coli found in a single bottle of Odwalla apple juice was identical to bacteria found in all 19 cases confirmed in the Seattle area since last week.

The number of confirmed cases linked to the Odwalla juice rose to 40 from 39, said a spokesman for the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta. Several dozen more cases are suspected, according to state authorities.

Kobayashi said it was too soon to say whether the outbreak had peaked. But he noted that the wave of sickness is far smaller than a 1993 outbreak linked to tainted hamburger meat that sickened 500 people and killed three young children in the Pacific Northwest.

Several children remained hospitalized including a 16-month-old girl in critical condition in Denver. Complications from E. coli O157:H7 include kidney failure that can cause permanent damage, and several afflicted children have required dialysis.
Greg Steltenpohl, chairman of Half Moon Bay, Calif.-based Odwalla Inc., said the company could have some reformulated juices back on store shelves by next week.

In addition to apple juice, the company voluntarily recalled 12 juice blends containing apple juice and three varieties containing carrot juice, which is produced on the same line at the company's Dinuba, Calif., plant.
"We expect to actually have products as early as next week that are made without apple juice that extend our line," Steltenpohl said at a news conference in Seattle.
Odwalla has no plans to resume making apple juice until more details are known about how its juice became tainted, Steltenpohl said.

Chief executive officer Stephen Williamson said Monday the company has no immediate plans to resume making carrot juice, which he described as a "more risky juice" because of its low acid content and the fact that carrots grow in the ground.

Steltenpohl said some retailers decided to pull all Odwalla products after epidemiologists established the apple juice link last week, but most of the company's 4,600 retailers have continued to stock its citrus drinks and bottled water.
